ABSTRACT

The present study deals with the synthesis of a novel $\mathrm { F e _ { 4 0 } M n _ { 1 9 } N i _ { 1 5 } A l _ { 1 5 } S i _ { 1 0 } C _ { 1 } }$ low-density high entropy steel (HES) processed through mechanical alloying (MA) and spark plasma sintering (SPS). The elemental powder was milled for 35 h, leading to the formation of multiphase structures i.e., BCC phase $( \mathsf { a } = 0 . 2 8 6$ nm; ${ \mathrm { c I 2 } } ) , \tau$ -brass type (a = 0.872 nm; cI52) and partially ordered B2-type $( \mathbf { a } = 0 . 2 9 0$ nm; cP2) phases with the trace amount of Si. The milled powder was found to be thermally stable up $\mathbf { t o } \sim 5 0 0 ^ { \circ } \mathbf { C } ,$ , however, the formation of Fe Si -type phase was evident at ${ \sim } 5 2 0 \ { ^ { \circ } } \mathrm { C } .$ The spark plasma sintered (SPSed) sample was able to retain the BCC phase $\mathbf { \rho } ( \mathbf { a } = 0 .$ .286 nm), γ-brass type $( \mathbf { a } = 0 . 8 7 2$ nm). B2 $( \mathsf { a } = 0 . 2 8 9$ nm) along with the formation of $\mathrm { F e } _ { 5 } \mathrm { S i } _ { 3 }$ type silicide phase ${ \mathfrak { a } } =$ ${ \bf b } = 0 . 6 6 7$ nm, c = 0.468 nm; hP16). These SPSed HES sample was found to have low density $( \sim 6 . 4 9 \pm 0 . 3 \mathrm { ~ g ~ }$ cm<sup>−</sup> <sup>3</sup>), high microhardness $( \sim 7 . 8 \pm 0 . 3$ GPa) and good compressive strength $( \sim 2 0 4 6 \ \pm$ 160 MPa) with an appreciable ductility of \~19%. The enhanced mechanical properties of the SPSed sample can be attributed to dual-phase microstructure i.e., BCC and B2 along with finer nano-sized silicide precipitates leading to dominant strengthening mechanisms (i.e., grain-boundary and dislocation strengthening). The experimental findings on phase evolution, thermal stability and mechanical properties of non-equiatomic HES were correlated with the various thermodynamic parameters. CALPHAD modelling and strengthening mechanisms. The significance of the present study is to design a high entropy steel containing the dual phase microstructures i.e., BCC as major phase and B2 as secondary phase, for giving rise to high mechanical strength and high temperature stability.
1. Introduction

The thrust for development of advanced materials having a synergy between strength and ductility has been evolving in the modern era of industrialization. The urge for high strength advanced materials led to the emergence of high entropy alloys (HEAs). The HEAs are usually disordered single-phase solid solution consisting of five or more major alloying elements in equiatomic or near-equiatomic compositions [1]. HEAs have allured the materials industries across the world due to their excellent mechanical and functional properties, and attracted attention from the research community [2]. These HEAs can be sub-categorized into various classes based on the types of alloying elements, microstructure and/or phases formed $\mathrm { i . e . , }$ , eutectic [3], non-equiatomic [4], precipitation strengthened [5], interstitial [6] HEAs, TRIP and TWIP HEAs [7,8], high entropy intermetallics [9], high entropy nano particles [10], and high entropy steels [11].

The HEAs are mainly prepared through liquid metallurgy route $\mathrm { i . e . , }$ vacuum arc melting or vacuum induction melting. However, this route has some limitations owing to porosity, segregation, difference in melting point and density among thealloying elements. Powder metal lurgy route $( \mathrm { i . e . , }$ mechanical alloying (MA) followed by sintering.) have overcome these problems and also easily produced the nanocrystalline materials with homogenous solid solution [12]. In addition, this tech nique can expand the solid solubility even in the immiscible alloys [13].

Spark plasma sintering (SPS) has become a popular technique for consolidation of mechanically alloyed powders. The high heating rate during SPS can be attributed to the generation of high-power current (pulsed). The samples consolidated by SPS can effectively retain the nanocrystalline features [14]. A few researchers revealed the nano crystalline nature of FCC phase along with $\mathrm { C r } _ { 7 } \mathrm { C } _ { 3 }$ in CrFeCoNi and CrMnFeCoNi HEAs processed by mechanical alloying (MA) and SPS [15]. These HEAs based composites’ mechanical properties were almost similar to those of a few advanced composites prepared by powder metallurgical processing $\mathrm { e . g . , C u { - S i C , A l _ { 2 } O _ { 3 } { - } W C { - } C O \ [ 1 6 , 1 7 ] } }$

The structural material used for high temperature applications ought to have phase stability up to higher temperatures. Therefore, it is of paramount importance to establish the thermal stability of these HEAs to ascertain two aspects i.e., phase transformation and the retention of nanosized structure. The CrFeCoNi HEA has revealed the high resistance to grain growth even at long duration of heat treatment at $9 0 0 ~ ^ { \circ } \mathrm { C }$ for 600 h [15]. Shivam et al. [18] synthesized AlCoCrFeMnNi HEA by mechano-chemical process and illustrated that the powder sample was thermally stable up to $5 0 0 ~ ^ { \circ } \mathrm { C }$ and afterwards encountered diffusional transformation to form minor fraction of intermetallics along with the parent phase at room temperature.

The use of carbon as an important interstitial alloying element has strong effect on the phase constitution and mechanical properties on steels, Ni-based and Co-based superalloys [19]. The addition of carbon in $\mathrm { F e _ { 4 0 . 4 } N i _ { 1 1 . 3 } M n _ { 3 4 . 8 } A l _ { 7 . 5 } C r _ { 6 } }$ [20], $\mathrm { F e } _ { 4 0 } \mathrm { M n } _ { 4 0 } \mathrm { C o } _ { 1 0 } \mathrm { C r } _ { 1 0 }$ [21], FeCoNiAl [22], Ni CoCuFeCr V $( x = 0 . 2 5$ , 0.5 mol) [23], FeCoNiCu [24], TiFeCoNiAl [25] and $\mathrm { C r _ { 2 0 } M n _ { 1 0 } F e _ { 3 5 } N i _ { 3 5 } }$ [26] HEAs showed excellent mechanical properties at room and high temperatures. Raabe et al. [27] studied the FeMnAl–C and FeMnAlSi–C high entropy steel having FCC structure and exhibiting good tensile ductility with nominal strength [27]. They explained the formation of different phases by varying the C and Mn content in the non equiatomic FeMnAlSi–C high entropy steel. The effect of C and Mn in the phase formation of FeMnAlSi–C high en tropy steel was shown efrom multiphase to single phase FCC solid so lution. Raabe and co-workers illustrated the formation of FCC structure strengthened by addition of Al and Si due to solid solution strengthening [27].

In the view of above, the present investigation envisages the prepa ration of a non-equiatomic low-density Fe Mn Ni Al Si C high entropy steel by MA and SPS possessing a multi-phase microstructure consisting of mainly BCC and B2 phases that may have greater strength with appreciable amount of ductility. The alloying behavior, thermal stability, microstructural and chemical analysis, mechanical properties (i.e., microhardness and compressive strength) during MA and SPS have been studied systematically. Further, the mechanical properties of these HES were understood with the help of various strengthening mechanisms.
2. Experimental details

The starting elemental powder of Fe, Ni, Mn, Al, Si and C (99.2% pure) was taken in appropriate proportion of $\mathrm { F e _ { 4 0 } M n _ { 1 9 } N i _ { 1 5 } A l _ { 1 5 } S i _ { 1 0 } C _ { 1 } }$ (at. %) (Fe-46.00%, Mn-21.50%, Ni-18.13%, Al-8.34%, Si-5.78%, C-0.25%; wt. %) and was milled in planetary ball mill (Model no. PM 400/ 2, Retsch) at the speed of 200 rpm. The ball to powder ratio was taken as 10:1. The milling was carried out in the tungsten carbide (WC) vials and with WC balls. To avoid oxidation, toluene was taken as a process control reagent during milling. To understand the phase evolution during milling, 2–3 g of milled powder was taken after every 5 h of milling. The milling was stopped intermittently for 20 min after every 1 h for avoiding any overheating. The 35 h milled powder was consoli dated by spark plasma sintering (Model no. Dr. Sinter SCM 1050, Japan) at a temperature of ${ 9 0 0 } ^ { \circ } \mathrm { C } ,$ pressure of 50 MPa, and heating rate of 100 $^ \circ \mathrm { C } .$ min<sup>−</sup> <sup>1</sup> with a holding time of 15 min. The diameter and thickness of the spark plasma sintered sample (SPSed) was \~30 mm and \~9 mm, respectively. The pellet was cleaned with the help of polisher to remove the graphite layer. The wire EDM machine (Medha enterprises, model no. EXPRESSCUT EX-2530) was used to cut the pellet into many pieces of dimensions (diameter = 4 mm and $\mathrm { h e i g h t } = 8$ mm) for further characterization and evaluation of mechanical properties. The differential scanning calorimeter (DSC) (Netzsch, DSC404 Pegasus) was used to study the thermal stability of milled powder. The 35 h milled powder was heated up to 1000 <sup>◦</sup>C with 20 K/min of heating rate under the nitrogen (N ) atomsphere. 35 h milled powder were encapsulated in a quartz tube and back filled with argon atmosphere for annealing it at higher temperatures. For better understanding of the thermal stability of this high entropy steel, 35 h milled sample was annealed for 1 h at diferent temperatures $\mathrm { ( i . e . , ~ } 4 0 0 \mathrm { ~ \textdegree C } , \mathrm { ~ } 5 0 0 \mathrm { ~ \textdegree C } , \mathrm { ~ } 6 0 0 \mathrm { ~ \textdegree C }$ and $8 0 0 ^ { \circ } \mathrm { C } )$ followed by water quenching. The alloying behavior during milling and phase formation after the SPS was ascertained by using high resolution X-Ray diffraction (XRD) (EMPYREAN, PANALYTICAL) with a Co-Kα source (operating voltage:40 kV; operating current:40 mA) with the scan rate of 5<sup>◦</sup> min<sup>−</sup> <sup>1</sup>. The XRD analysis of the annealed sample was done in the Rigaku X-Ray diffractometer (Cu- Kα source) operating at voltage of 40 kV and 15 mA of current with the scan rate of $5 ^ { \circ } \operatorname* { m i n } ^ { - 1 }$ The microstructural feature, chemical analysis and mapping of the milled powder at different milling time was examined using Evo 18 Carl Zeiss scanning electron microscope (SEM), and field emission scanning electron microscopee (FE-SEM) (FEI model no. Nova Nano SEM 450), both equipped with EDS detector. The microstructural study of the SPSed pellet was done with the help of FE-SEM (model no. Nova Nano SEM 450). The elemental analysis of the SPSed sample was performed by the EDS detector attached with SEM. For microstructural features, the SPSed samples were systematically polished and chemically etched with the 5% nitric acid and 95% methanol solution (Nital). For 35 h milled sample, structural analysis was done with the help of transmission electron microscope (TEM) (TECNAI $\mathrm { G } ^ { 2 } \mathrm { T } 2 0$ , FEI) operating at 200 kV. Electron Probe Micro Analyzer (EPMA) (CAMECA SXFive) was used for BSE imaging, quantitative point analysis and X-ray elemental mapping of the SPSed sample. The SPSed samples were carbon coated with 20 nm layer using LEICA-EM ACE200 instrument. Wavelength-dispersive spectrometry (WDS), LaB6 filament and TAP, PET, LIF, LPET and LTAP crystals were used at a voltage of 15 kV and current of 10 nA for the analyses. The acquisition, data processing and routine calibration were carried out using SxSAB version 6.1 and SX-Results software of CAMECA.

The XRD data of the milled samples, annealed and SPSed pellet were refined using Rietveld refinement method in the general structural analysis system (GSAS-II) [30] to determine the structural (lattice parameter) and microstructural (crystallite size and microstrain) pa rameters. The average crystallite size and isotropic microstrain was based on uniaxial model [30]. The crystallite size and lattice strain of the milled samples were calculated using the Rietveld refinement method with the help of GSAS-II (Table 2). The crystallite size was found to vary as a function of milling (Table 2). The crystallite size was found to be tuned in the range of \~13–17 nm and \~10–13 nm for BCC and γ-brass type phase respec tively. The crystallite size for Si decreased from 20 nm to 14 nm as milling extended from 25 h to 35 h. The lattice strain increased for all the phases as the milling time progressed. The increase in the lattice strain with milling is due to the atomic size difference between the individual elements, mechanical deformation in the powder and the increase in the fraction of grain boundary. Peak broadening and the decrease in diffraction peaks intensity with the milling are evident from Fig. 1(a). The reason is due to the lattice distortion leading to the induced lattice strain and extra grain refinement. The usual characteristics of the mill ing process and the combination of both the phenomenon contributes to the peak broadening. There is a slight change in the amount of phase fraction for the BCC and γ-brass type structure. The dislocation density shows the negligible change with the milling time and the values are displayed in Table 2.

Fig. 2(a–d) illustrates the size, shape and morphology of the milled powder at different milling time. Three different contrasts i.e., white, light and dark grey are clearly visible in the micrograph of 35 h milled sample. The size and shape of the powder particles are random and bulky at the early duration of the milling (as seen in Fig. 2(a)). The average particle sizes decreased drastically after 20 h of milling. The powder particles were becoming more homogenous as the milling increased. For 35 h milled samples, the mean particle size is 3–5 μm, and the size and shapes of the particles are different. The full area EDS analysis of the marked area (in Fig. 2(d)) is illustrated in Fig. 2(e), showing the peaks of all the elements in 35 h milled powder. Fig. 2(f–i) displays the histogram of particle size distribution at 10 h, 20 h, 30 h and 35 h, respectively. The particles size was measured using ImageJ soft ware. Fig. 2(j) shows the microstructure of the powder pellet (35 h) and its corresponding mapping and the point EDS. Table 3 lists the elemental composition of 35 h milled powder from different areas i.e., full area, spot 1 and spot 2. The light grey contrasts are rich in Fe and it corre sponds to BCC (ferritic phase) structure. The dark grey contrasts are rich in Mn and its stoichiometry are close to the γ-brass type structure. The chemical analysis also confirmed the formation of BCC (Fe-rich) and γ-brass type (Mn-rich) in 35-h milled powder.

The bright-field TEM image and its corresponding selected area diffraction pattern are shown in Fig. 3(a) and (b), respectively. The image shows that the nanocrystalline grains were formed after 35 h milled powder. The formation of ring pattern represents the poly crystalline nature of the alloy. The ring diffraction pattern correspond to the BCC crystal structure. The planes of (110), (200) and (211) of the BCC phase can be identified from the ring patterns.

4. Discussion
4.1. Alloying behavior and microstructure

The phase formation during milling and after spark plasma sintering was correlated with the thermodynamic parameters. Zhang et al. [42] proposed the three parameters for the prediction of disordered solid solution formation in the HEAs i.e., high configurational entropy $( \Delta S _ { \mathrm { c o n f } } ) ,$ , mixing enthalpy $\left( \Delta \mathrm { H } _ { \mathrm { m i x } } \right)$ and the size mismatch (δ). The $\Delta S _ { \mathrm { c o n f } } ,$ ΔH and δ parameters were calculated based upon the Boltzmann hypothesis, Miedema model and Zhang’s approach respectively [38,42]. The calculated values of thermodynamic parameter for the non-equiatomic high entropy steel and the criteria to form the solid solution are listed in Table 6. The values of the various parameter are well within the range of random solid solution formation criteria. Guo et al. [43] proposed some more parameters i.e., electronegativity (γ) valence electron concentration (VEC) and Ω for the prediction of solid solution formation in the multicomponent alloys. The VEC is used to predict the FCC/BCC or both the phase formation in the HEAs. The VEC is well within the range of dual-phase formation, and it forms the BCC type structure in the milled and SPSed sample of the present alloy. Al CoCrCuFeNi $( x = 0 . 4 5 , 1 , 2 . 5 , 5 \mathrm { a t . \ } \% )$ HEAs phase formation were discussed on the basis of mixing enthalpy, configurational entropy and size mismatch [44]. It was stated that the Al increased the B2 phase formation due to the high mixing enthalpy in the HEAs. It is also mentioned that the enthalpy of mixing in the HEAs system was preferred to form the ordering or clustering (formations of intermetallic com pound) [45]. Shivam et. al [46], discussed the phase formation in the non-equiatomic $\mathrm { F e } _ { 4 0 } \mathrm { C r } _ { 2 5 } \mathrm { N i } _ { 1 5 } \mathrm { A l } _ { 1 5 } \mathrm { C o } _ { 5 }$ medium entropy alloy in terms of binary mixing enthalphy and configurational entropy, which has formed the BCC and B2 structure. The B2 phase formation in the alloy was correlated with the binary enthalphy of mixing in Ni–Al which is the highest among the other pairs. In present alloy, the binary enthalpy between the Al–Fe, Al–Ni are highly negative. The values of the various possible pair of binary enthalphy are mention in the Table 1. To retain the solid solution in the HEAs at room temperature, the configurational entropy is not sufficient. The partially ordered B2-type structure in the alloy was formed due to the binary negative enthalpy. This parameters are well within the solid solution formation criteria. The criteria pro posed for the prediction of the disordered solid solution in the HEAs are based upon the results of the reported HEAs. However, some of the re ported HEAs suggested that the Zhang's criteria were neither necessary nor sufficient condition to predict the formation of disordered solid solution in the HEAs. This can only provide the basic idea to predict the phase formation criteria of disordered solid solution. Other than the thermodynamic parameters, the processing tenchique and atomic per centage of the indiviual elements also play an important role in the phase formation of the HEAs [45].

The diffraction intensity of the elemental peaks start diminishing as the milling time progresses, which indicates that the alloying is initiated. The dissolution of the individual elements during the milling is corre lated with the physicochemical properties and the values are compiled in Table 7. The dissolution of the elements depends on the lowest melting point and the brittleness of the HEAs [47]. But, carbon, being interstitial element dissolved faster as compared to the other alloying elements present which might be due to its less atomic size and high diffusivity [11,35]. As the milling proceeds, Al dissolved followed by Mn and Ni and formed the solid solution. This alloying rate depends upon the melting point and self-diffusion coeffecient of the indiviual elements [47]. Si remains undissolved after 35 h of milling was due to the lowest self-diffusion coefficient and non-metallic behavior [47]. The lattice parameter of the major BCC phase, formed during the milling is close to the ferritic iron (α-Fe) (acting as host lattice). Shivam et al. [18] explained the concept of the host lattice in HEAs system in terms of melting point and the bond strength of the elements present in the alloys.

4.2. Thermal stability

The phase evolution of the non-equiatomic HES at higher tempera ture are observed at ${ } ^ { 2 5 } \ ^ { \circ } \mathrm { C }$ such as BCC + γ-brass $\mathrm { t y p e } + { \bf B } \boldsymbol { 2 } + { \bf S } \mathrm { i }$ (undissolved). The alloy is thermally stable up $\mathbf { t o } \sim 5 0 0 \ { ^ \circ } \mathbf { C } . \ \mathrm { A t } \ 4 2 0 \ { ^ \circ } \mathbf { C } ,$ the phases observed to be stable are BCC + γ-brass $\mathrm { t y p e } + { \bf B } 2 \cdot \mathrm { t y p e }$ . But the phase fraction of the γ-brass type structure increased and some peaks were evolved. This type of transformation was also seen in the nonequiatomic $\mathrm { F e } _ { 4 0 } \mathrm { C r } _ { 2 5 } \mathrm { N i } _ { 1 5 } \mathrm { A l } _ { 1 5 } \mathrm { C o } _ { 5 }$ medium entropy alloy [46] and qua sicrystals $[ 2 9 , 4 8 , 4 9 ] .$ . At ${ 5 2 0 ~ ^ { \circ } \mathrm { C } } ,$ the phases are found to be BCC + γ-brass type + B2 and $\mathrm { F e } _ { 5 } \mathrm { { S i } _ { 3 } }$ type silicide. The silicide formation was also seen in the previously studied HEAs i.e., non-equiatomic FeMnNiTiAlSi–C [35], FeMnNiCrAlSi–C [11], AlCoCrFeNiSi [50] and AlCrFeMgNi [51] HEAs fabricated using the powder metallurgy route. The phase transformations occurred at higher temperature were due to the formation of metastable solid solution phase during milling. $\mathrm { F e _ { 3 6 } M n _ { 2 1 } C r _ { 1 8 } N i _ { 1 5 } A l _ { 1 0 } }$ high entropy alloy, the phases formed was BCC and B2. The alloy showed thermal stability of B2 phase at different heat treatment of the as-cast samples. The good thermal stability of the B2 phase was due to the strong bonding between the Ni–Al atoms and sluggish diffusion effect in the high entropy alloys [46,52]. In the pre sent alloy, the retention of the BCC and B2 phase after the various annealing condition and sintering was due to the strong bonding be tween the pairs of Fe–Al and Ni–Al, and sluggish diffusion effect. The formation of the silicide was due to the undissolved Si remaining after milling, and tendency of Fe and Mn to react with Si. The binary enthalpy of mixing between Fe–Si and Mn–Si is highly negative.

The present investigation envisaged to fabri cate a low-density high entropy steel possessing good microstructural stability as well as excellent mechanical properties having synergy with ductility. In spite of having excellent microstructural stability and me chanical properties, these SPSed HES were found to have a limited ductility of \~19%. Further, efforts towards tailoring the composition for designing and developing a low-density HES having excellent room temperature and high temperature properties may be a way forward for its potential structural applications.

Further, experiments were done to determine the mechanical properties $\mathrm { i . e . , }$ , microhardness, elastic modulus and compressive strength of the SPSed sample. The following conclusions can be drawn from the present study:

1. After 35 h of mechanical milling the phases formed were BCC, partially ordered B2-type and γ-brass type structure. The metastable alloy showed thermal stability up to $5 0 0 ^ { \circ } \mathrm { C } .$ . Afterwards, the $\mathrm { F e } _ { 5 } \mathrm { S i } _ { 3 ^ { - } }$ type intermetallic phases were formed at $5 2 0 ~ ^ { \circ } \mathrm { C } .$ . The formation of silicide at higher temperature could be due to higher binary negative enthlphy between the Fe–Si and atomic size mismatch, unfavourable for solid solution.

2. The BCC and B2-type phases retained after spark plasma sintering along with the formation of Fe<sub>5</sub>Si<sub>3</sub>-type silicide phase. The nano crystalline structure was observed even after annealing treatment and spark plasma sintering of the powder samples.

3. The dual phase structure i.e., BCC and B2 showed good strength i.e., microhardness $( 7 . 8 \ \pm \ 0 . 3 \ \mathrm { G P a } )$ and ultimate compressive stress (2046 ± 160 MPa) with an appreciable amount of compressive ductility (19%). The calculated values of strengthening based on materials modelling was close to the experimental values. The grain boundary and dislocation strengthening are found to be the domi nant mechanisms. The phase prediction through thermodynamic parameters and Thermo-Calc were correlated with the experimental results.
